articles.body: Services Top Right MSC Ajaccio omits Livorno call on MSE service October 20, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Hapag-Lloyd has announced that MSC Ajaccio voyage MM642A will omit its scheduled call at Livorno, Italy. The vessel, operating on the Mediterranean–South America East Coast (MSE) service, was originally scheduled to call at Livorno on 17 October 2026. According to Hapag-Lloyd, the omission is part of a schedule recovery measure. Import cargo rerouted through Barcelona Import cargo originally scheduled for discharge at Livorno will instead be discharged at Barcelona, Spain. The cargo will then connect with the next MSE vessel, MSC Meline voyage MM643A, which is scheduled to call on 23 October 2026. Export cargo originally planned for loading at Livorno will be transferred to the first available vessels, considering the revised routing and transit times. Hapag-Lloyd will send affected customers revised booking confirmations containing details of the respective loading vessels. Customers have also been advised to adjust their shipping documentation accordingly. articles.title: Maersk updates containerised vehicle booking requirements
articles.summary: Maersk has issued updated booking and acceptance requirements for vehicles transported in containers, following the introduction of dedicated UN numbers for battery-powered vehicles under IMDG Code Amendment 42-24. The requirements apply to new, used and damaged vehicles, including cars, motorbikes, e-bikes,...
articles.body: Maersk has issued updated booking and acceptance requirements for vehicles transported in containers, following the introduction of dedicated UN numbers for battery-powered vehicles under IMDG Code Amendment 42-24. The requirements apply to new, used and damaged vehicles, including cars, motorbikes, e-bikes, e-scooters, boats, forklifts, golf carts and aircraft. Whether a vehicle must be declared as dangerous goods depends on its power source and condition when it is handed over for transportation. Vehicle booking codes Customers must use the commodity code corresponding to the condition of the vehicle: Commodity code Description 004607 New vehicle, dangerous or non-dangerous goods 004608 Used vehicle, dangerous or non-dangerous goods 004609 Damaged vehicle, dangerous or non-dangerous goods Vehicles with unrepaired collision, structural, undercarriage or other material damage must be booked under commodity code 004609. Damaged electric vehicles may require an additional assessment before being accepted. Dangerous goods classifications The required UN number depends on the vehicle’s propulsion system: Vehicle type Classification Non-DG treatment under SP961 Petrol, diesel or gas powered UN 3166, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Hybrid, including plug-in hybrid UN 3166, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Fuel cell powered UN 3166, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Lithium-ion battery powered UN 3556, Class 9 Must be declared as dangerous goods Lithium metal battery powered UN 3557, Class 9 Must be declared as dangerous goods Sodium-ion battery powered UN 3558, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Other battery types, including lead-acid UN 3171, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met A vehicle may only be booked as non-dangerous goods when it satisfies every condition under Special Provision 961 of the IMDG Code. This includes having its fuel tank empty as defined by the Code. The forthcoming IMDG Code Amendment 43-26 will remove the current exemption available to hybrid vehicles. These vehicles will subsequently have to be declared as dangerous goods. The amendment may be applied voluntarily from January 2027 and will become mandatory in January 2028. Vehicles excluded from acceptance Maersk will not accept vehicles with damaged or defective batteries, flood or water damage, or signs or smells of leakage. Loose or spare batteries cannot be packed with a vehicle, although batteries installed in the vehicle are permitted. Vehicles are also prohibited from active reefer and non-operating reefer containers. Additionally, vehicles must not rest directly on or remain in contact with another vehicle inside the container. Loading and securing requirements The starter or auxiliary battery, normally the 12-volt battery, must be disconnected. Its terminals and cable ends must be insulated against short circuits. Vehicles must be switched off and cannot remain connected to a charger. Climate control, camping, security and other systems must also be deactivated. No cargo may be carried inside, on or attached to a vehicle. Standard equipment supplied by the manufacturer, including a spare wheel, jack and tool kit, may remain inside. Shippers are responsible for securing vehicles against movement in accordance with the IMO/ILO/UNECE Code of Practice for Packing of Cargo Transport Units. Maersk recommends that battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles be transported with a state of charge of no more than 30%. Vehicles declared as dangerous goods should carry only enough fuel to enter and leave the container. The carrier also recommends placing dangerous goods placards on all four sides of containers carrying vehicles, as requirements currently vary between ports. The next IMDG amendment is expected to introduce a formal placarding requirement. Non-compliant bookings or containers may be rejected or held, with any resulting expenses charged to the shipper. Goods discovered inside vehicles will be treated as undeclared cargo.

articles.title: Perenco brings ‘complex’ North Sea P&A and infrastructure removal campaign to an end
articles.summary: Perenco has wrapped up its decommissioning campaign, executing a P&A and infrastructure removal program in the UK North Sea.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 20, 2026 · 2 hours ago Perenco brings ‘complex’ North Sea P&A and infrastructure removal campaign to an end Perenco has wrapped up its decommissioning campaign, executing a P&A and infrastructure removal program in the UK North Sea. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Haeva Source: Petrodec Perenco UK, part of Anglo-French oil and gas player Perenco, alongside specialist contractor Petrodec, part of the Dixstone group, has undertaken a plug and abandonment (P&A) and infrastructure removal campaign in the Southern North Sea (SNS), which is seen as a step forward in the region's asset retirement activity. Perenco UK has confirmed the decommissioning of the Leman South (53/02a-15Y) and the Durango (48/21a-4z) subsea assets in the Southern North Sea, within a single campaign framework resulting in the plugging and abandonment of the wells and the removal of the associated subsea infrastructure. The company explains that these “highly complex” operations, which were completed in collaboration with Petrodec, were conducted safely and to the agreed timeframe using the contractor's Haeva jack-up vessel, building on recent experience gained from the Gawain , Arthur , and Davy subsea abandonment projects done using the same vessel. Jo White , Perenco UK SNS Managing Director, commented: “The Leman South and Durango campaigns were not routine P&A projects. They demonstrated Perenco's ability to deliver repeatable, large-scale, technically complex subsea well abandonment and infrastructure recovery using an innovative single campaign approach centred on Petrodec's Haeva, rather than relying exclusively on high-cost drilling rigs and standalone offshore projects. “I would like to thank our partners and the Perenco team who were involved in delivering some of the most technically demanding subsea well abandonment activities undertaken in the SNS.” This decommissioning milestone in the UK comes shortly after Perenco inked a gas deal for the Su Tu Trang Phase 2B project on Block 15-1 offshore Vietnam, set to supply more than 600 billion cubic feet (bcf) of gas over its life. articles.title: Major investments transform Gothenburg RoRo terminal
articles.summary: Gothenburg RoRo Terminal has undergone extensive development over the past three years, with a series of infrastructure upgrades delivering a modernised, more efficient and sustainable operation serving frequent sailings to key freight hubs in the UK and Central Europe. Cargo volumes handled over the quay increased...
articles.body: Gothenburg RoRo Terminal has undergone extensive development over the past three years, with a series of infrastructure upgrades delivering a modernised, more efficient and sustainable operation serving frequent sailings to key freight hubs in the UK and Central Europe. Cargo volumes handled over the quay increased five percent in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period last year, reflecting the positive impact of the investment programme. The terminal handles a broad mix of cargo including food, forest products, steel, electronics and automotive and engineering components. Its development coincides with growing intra-European shipping demand driven by geopolitical uncertainty, tariff disputes and global supply chain disruptions, prompting companies to seek regional, predictable transport solutions with frequent connections to European freight hubs. RoRo and short sea shipping are also increasingly valued as relief for congested inland transport corridors. The completed upgrades span nine areas. In 2024, 144,000 square metres of new terminal space were completed in the outer port area, the largest expansion since the terminal opened in the late 1970s. In 2023, Gothenburg RoRo Terminal took over operation of Arken Intermodal Terminal, adding 65,000 square metres and seven rail tracks enabling direct trailer transfers between trains and vessels. A cross-docking facility of 11,000 square metres for steel products was constructed in 2025, complemented by a 6,000 square metre covered cross-docking facility for forest products completed in 2024. The approach channel was widened and deepened during the 2022 to 2023 dredging season, enabling larger vessels and removing certain weather-related restrictions. Shipping lines CLdN and DFDS have deployed larger, more modern vessels on routes serving the terminal. Berth 710 was upgraded in 2026 with an extended quay projection and new ramp to increase loading capacity for larger vessels. A green hydrogen refuelling station was established adjacent to the terminal in 2024 serving both hydrogen-powered trucks and terminal vehicles. The eastern quay is also set to be upgraded to accommodate larger, more modern vessels. Jacob Minnhagen, Senior Market Development Manager at the Port of Gothenburg, described the terminal as having a genuine 2.0 feel following the rapid pace of development. Maria Franksen, CEO of Gothenburg RoRo Terminal, described the volume growth as a positive indication that the long-term, focused approach to developing capacity, quality and efficiency is paying off, while expressing commitment to continued improvement to meet the current and future needs of Swedish industry.

articles.summary: New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant BW LPG is cashing in again on strong secondhand values, agreeing to sell an 18-year-old VLGC for more than $80m as it presses ahead with a major fleet renewal programme. The company’s 52%-owned subsidiary, BW LPG India, has signed an agreement to sell the 2008-built, 84,601...
articles.body: Asia Gas BW LPG India offloads 18-year-old VLGC for over $80m Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 0 1 minute read BW LPG India BW LPG India New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant BW LPG is cashing in again on strong secondhand values, agreeing to sell an 18-year-old VLGC for more than $80m as it presses ahead with a major fleet renewal programme. The company’s 52%-owned subsidiary, BW LPG India, has signed an agreement to sell the 2008-built, 84,601 cu m BW Loyalty for continued trading. BW LPG said the vessel had fetched a price in the low-$80m range, with the transaction expected to generate a gain of approximately $52m and net cash proceeds of around $66m after taxes and transaction costs. Both figures are calculated on a 100% ownership basis, rather than BW LPG’s attributable 52% stake in the Indian subsidiary. The ship will remain on its existing time charter before changing hands, with the sale expected to be completed by December. The buyer has not been disclosed. The latest disposal adds to a string of profitable sales by the Indian operation. In August, BW LPG India agreed to sell the 2007-built B W Birch , expecting approximately $64m in net cash proceeds and a $37m gain. That followed the July sale of another 2007-built VLGC, BW Elm , which generated around $64m in cash and a $36m book gain. Including BW Loyalty, the three announced transactions represent approximately $194m in net cash proceeds and $125m in gains on a 100% basis, although the latest sale has yet to close. The disposals come as BW LPG embarks on its largest newbuilding programme in years. In May, the company contracted eight 90,000 cu m panamax VLGCs at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries for approximately $940m, with deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The group subsequently raised $300m through a convertible bond offering in September, with the proceeds earmarked partly for financing the newbuilding programme. articles.title: LNG Canada entrusts Técnicas Reunidas with €200M+ EPCM deal
articles.summary: Técnicas Reunidas has secured work on LNG Canada's Coastal GasLink Phase 2, fueling the engineering firm's North American growth.
articles.body: Project & Tenders October 20, 2026 · 3 hours ago LNG Canada entrusts Técnicas Reunidas with €200M+ EPCM deal Técnicas Reunidas has secured work on LNG Canada's Coastal GasLink Phase 2, fueling the engineering firm's North American growth. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email LNG Canada Técnicas Reunidas, a Spanish-based engineering contractor, is cementing its footprint in North America, with an engineering, procurement and construction management (EPCM) assignment worth more than €200 million for Phase 2 of the Coastal GasLink pipeline awarded by LNG Canada, a joint venture featuring Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation, and KOGAS. This four-year contract, which TR Canada E&C won for EPCM services related to Phase 2 of Coastal GasLink (CGL) in British Columbia on Canada’s west coast, deepens a partnership that began during the LNG Canada project's initial front-end engineering design (FEED) stages, marking another win for the Spanish engineering firm's North American growth strategy. CGL Phase 2 will be delivered through an integrated execution model, with LNG Canada leading project construction as Phase 2 Execution Manager and TR Canada E&C providing the EPCM services, while CGL will remain the owner, operator, and permit holder of the pipeline and associated facilities. The contract award comes only weeks after LNG Canada reached its Phase 2 final investment decision (FID) to advance the next stage of development of this British Columbia-based project of national significance. The project includes the construction of five additional compressor stations, as well as modifications to both existing and planned facilities at various points along the pipeline route. Related Articles Business & Finance Shell bets big on Canada with go-ahead for LNG project expansion, doubling capacity to 28 mtpa 3 min read Técnicas Reunidas’ scope entails the detail engineering, procurement, and construction management services, with an expected execution period of over four years, representing a significant milestone in the strengthening of the firm’s services business. The newly awarded contract with LNG Canada adds to the company’s extensive experience in midstream projects, which includes 30,000 kilometers of oil and gas pipelines and more than 35 large compression projects worldwide. The award reinforces Técnicas Reunidas’ commitment to the North American market, a cornerstone of its current SALTA Strategic Plan. The firm has already identified a pipeline of potential projects worth €28 billion in the North American market. A significant portion consists of around a dozen large-scale combined-cycle power plants, primarily aimed at meeting the high and growing energy needs resulting from the boom in large data centers being developed in the region. All three charter agreements will now remain in effect until 31 December 2027. Godby Shipping said the extensions provide operational continuity for the vessels and their crews while continuing the company’s long-standing cooperation with DFDS. articles.summary: China's military said on Tuesday it had sent forces to watch a US warship that "illegally" entered waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, while further north in the waterway, Taiwan reported a standoff with a Chinese vessel.

REUTERS/Francis Malasig/Pool/File Photo By Liz Lee and Ben Blanchard BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct 20 (Reuters) – China’s military said on Tuesday it had sent forces to watch a US warship that “illegally” entered waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, while further north in the waterway, Taiwan reported a standoff with a Chinese vessel. China views almost all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite overlapping claims by Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam, with recent tension most pronounced between Beijing and Manila. The Chinese military’s Southern Theatre Command said the USS Charleston “illegally intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands without Chinese government approval in the early hours of Tuesday. “The US action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability,” it said in a statement. “The US side should immediately cease such activities.” China’s navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the ship, it added. The US Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It generally refers to such missions as “freedom of navigation operations,” though its last known one in the South China Sea was more than a year ago. A Philippines’ military spokesperson said the US ship “did not trespass into ‘Chinese territory’,” adding that no nation had the authority to require prior permission for “lawful transit through international waters.” Last month, a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine boat on a refueling mission near the same shoal, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. China blamed the collision on the Philippine side. China and the Philippines, which has a mutual defense treaty with the US, both contest sovereignty over Sabina Shoal and the entire Spratly Islands archipelago. PRATAS STANDOFF In a separate incident on Tuesday at the top end of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said a Chinese Coast Guard ship had entered restricted waters near the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands. The Taiwan Coast Guard said its ship the “Taichung” was dispatched to warn away the Chinese boat, while both sides broadcast messages to each other. The Chinese ship broadcast that “the so-called Republic of China does not exist,” referring to Taiwan’s official name, while the Taiwanese ship broadcast back that “the Republic of China, Taiwan, is a sovereign and independent country,” Taiwan’s Coast Guard said, adding the standoff was continuing. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The office said last week that Taiwan must “bear the consequences” of its Coast Guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas . The Pratas Islands lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong, but are only lightly defended and security is the responsibility of Taiwan’s Coast Guard. China has also been stepping up coast guard activity around Taiwan, including off the island’s east coast, causing concern in Western capitals. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory. Speaking at a forum in Taipei on Tuesday, the chair of a review commission appointed by the US Congress said Chinese coast guard patrols to the east of Taiwan were “highly destabilizing.” Addressing the same event, Taiwan’s National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu said China had no legal claim to the waters off the island’s east. articles.body: PD Ports has opened a new multi-million-pound marine facility at Cargo Fleet Wharf, within Teesport Commerce Park in Middlesbrough, UK. The three-storey building brings the company’s marine operations and engineering teams together at one location. It replaces facilities at Vulcan Street that had been in use since the 1960s. The investment will support the safe movement of vessels along the River Tees and at the Port of Hartlepool. New facilities improve vessel maintenance The new building includes a specialist workshop for maintaining and repairing marine vessels. For the first time, PD Ports can lift smaller vessels directly from the river onto the quay and move them indoors for maintenance. This will provide safer working conditions for engineers and make repairs more efficient. PD Ports designed and delivered much of the project through its own engineering teams, working with local suppliers where needed. As the Statutory Harbour Authority, the company is responsible for keeping the River Tees and the Port of Hartlepool safe for navigation. Its marine teams carry out dredging, hydrographic surveys, maintenance of navigational aids and oil spill response operations. Their work helps keep shipping channels open and supports commercial vessels and terminal operators. He said the company would continue investing in the infrastructure and expertise needed to maintain safe navigation. The new facility is part of PD Ports’ wider investment in marine operations. The company has also invested £23 million in the Emerald Duchess , which forms part of its marine fleet. The Port of Tees and Hartlepool is the sixth-largest port in the UK by cargo volume and the largest in North East England.

While announcing in a unanimous vote to accelerate LNG infrastructure development through a landmark blanket authorization program, the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission emphasized the proposal would streamline permitting, speed energy infrastructure development, and deliver unprecedented regulatory certainty for project developers. FERC’s notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR) intends to establish an LNG blanket authorization program to allow eligible activities at LNG facilities to proceed without case-specific authorization orders under Sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act (NGA). This program is modeled on the commission’s 40-year blanket certificate program for interstate natural gas pipelines. Laura V. Swett , FERC’s Chairman, commented: “American energy dominance requires us to build and maintain the energy infrastructure our country needs without unnecessary delay. I am immensely proud of FERC’s historic proposal. “It shows what can be possible when we combine regulatory excellence, robust safeguards, and a firm commitment to the nation’s energy future. Consumers benefit when more energy infrastructure is online, dependable, and affordable, and FERC is helping make that future a reality.” Related Articles Fossil Energy FERC easing rules to expedite construction of natural gas projects 3 min read The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission is proposing a three-tiered authorization framework under which certain activities could proceed automatically, with periodic reporting, while others would require advance notice to FERC. Interested parties will have 60 days after the NOPR is published in the Federal Register to submit comments. Under the automatic authorization umbrella are activities that would not increase an LNG plant’s authorized capacity, expand the authorized vertical or horizontal extents within the plant’s footprint, or cause flows, levels, volumes, pressures, temperatures, compositions, or loads to exceed applicable design limits. A 60-day prior notice covers activities that may increase the plant’s authorized capacity but remain within the plant’s footprint and do not cause operating conditions to exceed the design limits of the affected or remaining facilities. articles.title: Big Data in Logistics: What to Fix Before You Invest
articles.summary: Logistics is one of the most data-rich industries in the world. Every shipment generates location pings, weight records, customs entries, temperature logs, driver behavior data, fuel consumption metrics, and customer delivery confirmations. A mid-size logistics operator running a few hundred vehicles and a handful of...
articles.body: Logistics is one of the most data-rich industries in the world. Every shipment generates location pings, weight records, customs entries, temperature logs, driver behavior data, fuel consumption metrics, and customer delivery confirmations. A mid-size logistics operator running a few hundred vehicles and a handful of warehouses produces more raw operational data in a week than most industries generate in a quarter. And yet, the majority of that data goes unused. Not because logistics companies don’t want to use it — most do, and many have invested significant budget into big data initiatives to prove it. The problem is that having data and being ready to extract value from it are two different things. The gap between them is where most big data investments in logistics quietly fail. According to GM Insights , the big data in logistics market was valued at $4.3 billion in 2023 and is growing at over 21.5% annually, driven by demand for supply chain visibility, cost reduction, and predictive operations. 98% of 3PL companies believe big data analytics makes decision-making easier. DB Schenker reported a 15% reduction in operational costs after implementing a big data analytics platform. DHL has 92% of its facilities equipped with digital solutions including big data analytics. The opportunity is real. But so are the failure modes — and most of them are invisible until significant money has already been spent. This article covers the foundational problems logistics companies need to fix before a big data investment can deliver on its promise. The Fundamental Problem: Data Volume Is Not Data Readiness The most common misconception in logistics big data projects is equating data volume with data value. Logistics operations generate enormous quantities of data. The assumption — rarely stated explicitly but almost always present — is that scale equals opportunity, and that deploying analytics infrastructure on top of existing data will automatically surface the insights the business needs. It doesn’t. And the reason is straightforward: most logistics data environments are not built for analysis. They are built for operations. TMS platforms record shipments. WMS platforms manage warehouse movements. ERP systems handle invoicing and procurement. Fleet telematics systems capture vehicle data. Carrier APIs feed tracking events. Each of these systems was designed to serve its specific operational function — not to be analyzed alongside the others. The data they produce is often inconsistent in format, contradictory in definition, incomplete in coverage, and siloed in ways that make cross-system analysis technically painful and analytically unreliable. According to a systematic literature review published in Springer’s Forum journal in 2026, the persistent challenges in big data logistics adoption include data governance, infrastructure requirements, and the limited digital maturity of many operators — regardless of the volume of data they generate. Volume is not the constraint. Readiness is. Before investing in big data analytics infrastructure, logistics companies need an honest audit of whether their underlying data environment can actually support the analyses they want to perform. Most discover it cannot — at least not without foundational work first. What to Fix: The Six Pre-Investment Priorities 1. Data Integration and Fragmentation The average mid-to-large logistics operator runs between eight and fifteen distinct software systems that generate operational data. These systems were typically acquired at different times, from different vendors, for different operational purposes. Their data models are inconsistent. Their timestamps may be in different time zones. Their definitions of core concepts — “shipment,” “delivery,” “exception,” “on time” — often differ in ways that are not immediately obvious but matter enormously when you try to analyze across them. Data fragmentation is consistently cited as the primary obstacle to big data value in logistics. Before investing in analytics platforms or ML models, organizations need to invest in integration — building the pipelines, mappings, and data models that allow data from disparate operational systems to be combined and analyzed coherently. This is unglamorous work. It is also the work that determines whether every subsequent analytics investment succeeds or fails. The integration layer does not need to be perfect before analytics can begin. But it needs to be coherent — meaning the data flowing into any analytics system is consistent in definition, reliable in coverage, and trustworthy enough to make decisions against. 2. Data Quality: The Silent Investment Killer Poor data quality is the single most common reason big data initiatives in logistics fail to deliver expected returns. Not technology selection. Not vendor capability. Not model complexity. Data quality. A demand forecasting model trained on shipment data that includes 15% duplicate records will produce systematically biased forecasts. A route optimization system fed GPS coordinates with irregular recording intervals will generate recommendations that don’t reflect actual road conditions. A predictive maintenance system trained on telematics data with inconsistent vehicle ID mapping will attribute maintenance events to the wrong vehicles. Gartner projects that organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data. In logistics, AI-ready data means consistent identifiers across systems, complete records for the events being analyzed, accurate timestamps, and validation rules that catch entry errors before they corrupt analytical outputs. The investment required to improve data quality is real — it involves both technical work (deduplication, standardization, validation pipelines) and organizational work (training, process changes, accountability for data entry quality). But it is an investment that pays returns across every analytics use case, not just the one that motivated it. Organizations that clean their data once benefit from that investment indefinitely. 3. Real-Time Data Infrastructure One of the most commercially significant big data applications in logistics — operational decision-making — requires real-time or near-real-time data access. Routing decisions, exception management, carrier selection, warehouse slot allocation, and last-mile coordination all benefit from data that reflects current operational state, not yesterday’s batch export. Most logistics data environments are built on batch processing architectures that aggregate and move data on overnight or hourly schedules. For historical analysis and planning, this is adequate. For operational decision support, it is not. Before investing in real-time analytics applications, logistics operators need to assess whether their data infrastructure actually supports the latency requirements those applications need. Implementing streaming data pipelines — using technologies like Apache Kafka for event ingestion and Apache Flink for stream processing — is a significant infrastructure investment. But it is a prerequisite for the operational use cases that deliver the fastest and most measurable ROI from big data in logistics. 4. Governance: Who Owns the Data? Data governance is the most consistently underinvested area in logistics big data programs — and its absence is one of the most reliable predictors of program failure. Governance is not a compliance exercise. In a logistics context, it is the organizational infrastructure that answers the practical questions every analytics program depends on: Who is responsible for the accuracy of shipment records? When a TMS and a carrier tracking system report different delivery times, which one is authoritative? Who has the authority to change data definitions in the WMS, and how are those changes communicated to analytics systems downstream? Without answers to these questions — embedded in policies, ownership structures, and operational processes — analytics programs make decisions based on data whose provenance and reliability are unclear. This leads to low confidence in analytical outputs, resistance from operational teams who don’t trust the numbers, and the death-by-skepticism that ends more logistics analytics programs than technology failures do. Governance investment before analytics investment pays off in user adoption. Operational teams that trust the data trust the analytics. Teams that don’t trust the data ignore the analytics — no matter how technically sophisticated they are. 5. Organizational Capability to Act on Insights Big data analytics in logistics does not create value by surfacing insights. It creates value when someone acts on those insights, and when the operational processes exist to translate analytical outputs into operational changes. This sounds obvious. In practice, it is the gap that many logistics operators discover only after deploying analytics infrastructure. A demand forecasting system that produces more accurate shipment volume predictions is worthless if the procurement and capacity planning processes that should use those predictions are not adjusted to incorporate them. A route optimization recommendation engine that generates better routes is worthless if drivers override its recommendations without consequence and dispatchers don’t have the authority to enforce compliance. Before investing in analytics, logistics operators need to map the operational decisions the analytics is intended to improve, identify who makes those decisions, and assess whether the organizational processes and authority structures exist to translate better information into different behavior. If they don’t, the analytics investment will generate reports that no one acts on — an expensive way to produce documents. 6. A Clear Definition of What Success Looks Like The final pre-investment fix is deceptively simple: knowing what you are trying to achieve, specifically enough to measure whether you achieved it. “Better supply chain visibility” is not a success definition. “Reduce average exception resolution time from 4.2 hours to 2 hours across our top 10 carrier lanes” is. “Improve our data” is not a success definition. “Reduce duplicate shipment records in our TMS from 12% to under 2% within six months” is. Big data investments in logistics that begin with vague goals consistently end with ambiguous outcomes — which makes it impossible to evaluate ROI, justify continued investment, or identify what needs to change. Organizations that define specific, measurable operational outcomes before they begin consistently make better technology choices, because the technology selection is driven by the specific capability required to achieve the defined outcome. Where Big Data Creates Real Value in Logistics — Once Foundations Are in Place The pre-investment fixes above are not the exciting part of the big data conversation. The exciting part is what becomes possible once those foundations are in place. Route optimization using real-time traffic, weather, and telematics data reduces fuel costs and improves delivery reliability — UPS eliminated over 100 million miles annually from its fleet using data-driven routing, generating approximately $400 million in fuel savings. Predictive maintenance on fleet and warehouse equipment reduces unplanned downtime by 30–50% in documented deployments. Demand forecasting accuracy improvements reduce both overstock and stockout events, directly improving margin in inventory-intensive logistics operations. Carrier performance analytics enable data-driven carrier selection that reduces exception rates and claims costs. Last-mile optimization using historical delivery data, customer behavior signals, and real-time operational state improves both delivery success rates and cost-per-delivery. Average annual cost savings in logistics operations from big data implementations reach $1.2 million, according to recent industry benchmarks. These returns are achievable — but they are not achievable without the foundational work that makes analytics trustworthy, integrated, and actionable. Working with the Right Partner The foundational work described in this article — integration, data quality, real-time infrastructure, governance, organizational alignment, and success definition — is not glamorous. It is also not optional. It is the work that determines whether a big data investment generates returns or generates reports. Organizations that attempt to skip the foundational work in favor of deploying impressive analytics technology consistently spend more and achieve less than those who invest in the foundations first. The pattern is predictable: a sophisticated platform deployed on fragmented, low-quality data produces outputs that operational teams don’t trust, leading to adoption failure and eventual program abandonment. Working with experienced partners who have delivered logistics analytics programs from data infrastructure through production deployment significantly reduces the risk of the common failure modes. The team at InData Labs , for instance, often finds that the first conversation with a new logistics client isn’t about technology at all — it’s about whether the data feeding that technology is actually trustworthy. That diagnostic step, done honestly before any platform is selected or any model is built, is what separates engagements that generate real operational returns from ones that produce dashboards nobody uses. The logistics operators generating real value from big data in 2026 are not the ones with the most data or the most sophisticated technology. They are the ones who built the foundations first, defined outcomes clearly, and invested in analytics where the operational processes existed to act on what the data revealed. That sequence matters more than any technology choice. Big data in logistics is genuinely transformational — for organizations that are actually ready for it.

articles.body: Carbon Capture Usage & Storage October 20, 2026 · 4 hours ago EU backs cross-border CO2 transport and storage project with €223 million NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Aker BP Aker BP and Höegh Evi have secured €223 million from the European Union Innovation Fund for a large-scale CO2 transport and storage (CCS) project that will permanently store CO2 on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS) from European industry. The Atlas project, which combines regional CO2 aggregation, large-scale low-pressure maritime transport and offshore storage, has a design capacity of 6 million tons of CO2 per year, with potential to expand beyond 10 million tons as the European CCS market develops. Confirmed as an EU Project of Mutual Interest (PMI 13.17) this April, being recognized as cross-border European CO2 infrastructure, the project has completed the feasibility phase and progressed into the Select phase, targeting a final investment decision (FID) in 2028 and first injection from 2031. "Atlas demonstrates how regional aggregation and large-scale low-pressure shipping can efficiently connect industrial regions to permanent CO₂ storage. This flexible maritime model can expand as the European CCS market develops," said Nils Jakob Hasle , EVP Clean Energy at Höegh Evi. According to Höegh Evi, CO2 will be aggregated at regional export hubs close to industrial clusters and transported by dedicated carriers to the Atlas storage site in the Norwegian North Sea. The CO2 will be injected through subsea infrastructure into a saline aquifer for storage more than 2,000 meters below the seabed at the storage site located in the Aker BP-operated EXL011 (80% Aker BP, 20% ORLEN Upstream Norway). "Europe needs safe and cost-effective permanent CO₂ storage. Atlas is designed to provide European industries with significant storage capacity on the Norwegian Continental Shelf and capture economies of scale needed to reduce CCS value chain costs," said Ørjan Jentoft , CCS Asset Manager at Aker BP. articles.body: ProRail has awarded VolkerRail a contract to redevelop the Waalhaven Zuid rail yard at the Port of Rotterdam, increasing its capacity to handle longer freight trains. The contract was signed on October 15, 2026. Construction is scheduled to begin in late 2026 and continue until the end of 2028. The project will improve rail freight operations at the port, supporting growing demand for cargo transport between Rotterdam and inland destinations. Rail yard to accommodate 740-metre container trains The redevelopment will provide six tracks capable of handling freight and container trains up to 740 metres long. It will also add 12 locomotive parking spaces and upgrade the existing railway infrastructure, including further electrification. ProRail plans to improve the separation of secured and unsecured areas. This will allow train movements and shunting operations to take place more safely and efficiently. The project is expected to increase capacity at Waalhaven Zuid and improve its ability to handle growing freight volumes. Freight operations to continue during construction One of the main challenges is completing the redevelopment while keeping rail freight services running wherever possible. Space at the rail yard is limited, and the project must meet technical, environmental and permitting requirements. To address these challenges, ProRail has reached agreements with the Municipality of Rotterdam and the Port of Rotterdam Authority to secure temporary working space near the site. ProRail and VolkerRail will now finalise the construction arrangements. Rail operators, shippers and other stakeholders will receive updates on the works and any expected disruption. The project also receives financial support from the European Commission. According to ProRail, the investment will help Waalhaven Zuid meet increasing demand for rail freight services to and from the Port of Rotterdam.

articles.title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
articles.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January...
articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Regulatory UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 122 1 minute read UK Government UK Government The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January 2025, had imposed a substantially greater administrative workload on shipowners and regulators than initially anticipated. The 22-page report identifies difficulties with reporting deadlines, fuel certification, emissions calculations and compliance pooling arrangements. Some operators missed deadlines despite meeting their operational obligations, while inconsistencies between verification systems created additional work. The Chamber wants the UK government to establish a fully tested ship-level monitoring and reporting system before introducing compliance obligations. It is also pushing for fuel-neutral regulation, realistic emissions targets based on fuel availability and infrastructure readiness, and flexibility for owners and operators to meet their obligations without unnecessary commercial disruption. Peter Aylott, the Chamber’s director of policy, said the government had an opportunity to learn from the EU’s experience rather than create another regulatory system that increased costs and complexity. The paper also calls for close alignment with emerging International Maritime Organization requirements to avoid duplicate certification, reporting and verification obligations. The intervention comes as the Department for Transport prepares to consult on a domestic maritime fuel standard, with the consultation expected later this year. Britain’s maritime decarbonisation strategy, unveiled in March 2025, targets a 30% reduction in domestic shipping’s lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, rising to 80% by 2040 and zero by 2050, against a 2008 baseline. The government has identified fuel regulation and emissions pricing as central measures for meeting those targets. articles.body: Europe Finance and Insurance Tankers Marinakis tanker venture locks down $930m for 11 VLCC newbuilds Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 283 1 minute read Capital Group Capital Group Greek shipowner Capital Tankers has lined up $930.3m in financing for 11 VLCC newbuildings under construction in China and South Korea, making further headway in funding its expanding crude tanker fleet. The Evangelos Marinakis-backed company has signed four financing arrangements since late September, covering vessels booked at Hanwha Ocean, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Co (DSIC) and Hengli Shipbuilding. The largest portion, totalling $450.6m, covers five 307,000 dwt VLCCs at DSIC. Three vessels are being financed at between $89.6m and $90.9m each under an October agreement, with another two securing $89.6m apiece. Capital Tankers has also arranged $241.8m for three 320,000 dwt LNG dual-fuel-ready VLCCs at South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean, alongside $237.9m for three 306,000 dwt vessels at Hengli in China. The Hanwha financing carries a five-year repayment schedule, while the Chinese yard packages are structured over ten years. All include substantial balloon payments at maturity, ranging from $39.7m to $60.9m per vessel. The company has not identified the financing providers. Separately, Capital Tankers has disclosed a $64.5m sale-and-leaseback arrangement for its newly delivered 155,348 dwt LNG dual-fuel suezmax Amor , built at New Times Shipbuilding in China. The financing, arranged earlier this year, runs to October 2033, with a $40m final payment. The latest financing commitments follow Capital Tankers’ $500m Oslo private placement earlier this year, which was upsized after strong investor demand as the Marinakis group brought its crude tanker business to the public market. The owner has since continued adding tonnage. In June, it acquired three VLCC newbuilding contracts at Hengli from parent Capital Maritime & Trading at $122m apiece, with deliveries scheduled for the second half of 2027. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Dutch inland shipping duo expands into Belgium with new chartering venture Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 162 1 minute read TriBarge TriBarge Dutch inland shipping companies Amer Shipping and Van de Graaf & Meeusen have joined forces to establish a new chartering business in Antwerp, backed by a fresh dry cargo newbuilding order at Concordia Damen. The two family-owned operators have launched TriBarge to target Belgian and French shippers, combining their existing networks and vessel capacity with plans for joint fleet investment. The new company will handle dry cargo, general cargo and breakbulk movements across the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region, German canals, the Moselle and inland waterways reaching Basel. Through its partnership with Stream Shipping, an existing venture between Amer Shipping and German cooperative MSG eG, TriBarge will also be able to serve destinations as far as the Black Sea. The partners have already contracted an 85 m dry cargo vessel at Concordia Damen. The newbuilding, to be named Porta Sud , is scheduled to enter service in the second half of 2027 and will be designed to access smaller inland ports, tributaries and canals as well as major rivers. The move comes just weeks after Amer Shipping returned to Concordia Damen for another two 110 m CDS Dry Cargo newbuildings, lifting its programme of shallow-draught vessels to six. Those ships are scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2027 and the second quarter of 2028. The first, AM Lianova , will join Stream Shipping, while the second will enter Amer’s own fleet. Amer Shipping operates a network of close to 60 vessels, transporting around 9m tonnes of cargo annually across the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Germany and Switzerland. Its new partner, Van de Graaf & Meeusen, is a Ridderkerk-based inland shipping and chartering specialist with a fleet of pushboats and barges serving the dry bulk market. TriBarge will operate from Antwerp’s Tweede Havendok, with Devin van Dam joining as a chartering broker on November 1. Another Belgian broker is expected to join in the second quarter of 2027. articles.title: Seaborne coal trade rebounds as Asian energy crisis reshapes global flows
articles.summary: Global seaborne coal trade has returned to growth in 2026, reversing last year’s decline as disruption to LNG supplies and shifting Asian demand patterns reshape international coal flows, according to new research from global shipbroker IFCHOR GALBRAITHS (IG). Seaborne coal exports increased by 3% year-on-year in...
articles.body: Seaborne coal trade rebounds as Asian energy crisis reshapes global flows in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 20/10/2026 Global seaborne coal trade has returned to growth in 2026, reversing last year’s decline as disruption to LNG supplies and shifting Asian demand patterns reshape international coal flows, according to new research from global shipbroker IFCHOR GALBRAITHS (IG). Seaborne coal exports increased by 3% year-on-year in January–September 2026, following a 4% contraction in 2025. The recovery has been driven partly by disruption to LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, prompting Asian power utilities to increase coal purchases. IG’s new Coal Markets Companion Report reveals a market increasingly characterised by divergent regional demand and changing trade routes. Between March and September, Asian seaborne thermal coal imports were broadly flat at around 550 million tonnes, as lower purchases by China (-7%) and India (-10%) were matched by a rise of around 10% in the rest of Asia, led by South Korea, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Japan and Vietnam. Laura Gomez, Research & Advisory, IFCHOR GALBRAITHS, commented: “The recovery in seaborne coal trade is particularly interesting because it is happening despite falling imports into China and India. Demand is shifting towards other Asian markets, partly in response to LNG supply disruption, while changes in sourcing are affecting established trade routes. It demonstrates why we need to look beyond headline coal consumption figures to understand what is happening in seaborne trade.” On the supply side, Indonesia, responsible for approximately 47% of global seaborne thermal coal trade, saw exports fall 7% in January–September, including a 16% decline in the third quarter. IG forecasts Indonesian coal exports easing to approximately 450 million tonnes by 2030. Meanwhile, metallurgical coal followed a different trajectory, with global seaborne trade increasing 10% year-on-year in January–September, supported by stronger Chinese demand. Australian metallurgical coal exports rose 13%, with shipments to China almost doubling. IG launches Coal 360 The findings accompany the launch of Coal 360, IG’s latest Commodities 360 market intelligence service, building on its existing Iron Ore, Agri and Bauxite research. Coal 360 provides detailed analysis of global thermal and metallurgical coal markets, covering production, exports, trade flows, ports, vessel deployment and forecasts, supported by regular updates and access to IG’s Research & Advisory team. articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Down on the surface in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index fell 6.97 points (3.0%) to close at 224.91, pulled down by a broad equity-market selloff — the S&P 500 lost 1.95%, its biggest weekly drop since June. But the sector’s internals were far stronger than the headline: the median constituent fell just 0.43%, and the weighted index (wUPI) actually rose 2.87%, so the decline was concentrated in a few heavier names rather than reflecting genuine sector weakness. Breadth was 10:11 on above-average volume. Two Asian names led with double-digit gains — MISC +15.4% (fleet expansion with QatarEnergy and a 20-year Petronas newbuild order) and Pan Ocean +11% (breaking through all key resistance) — while the oil & gas majors surged to fresh highs: BP +8.6%, Shell +6.5% and Chevron +6.14%. The drag came from COSCO, down almost 15%, with FLEX LNG and Dynagas each off 8% and Golar −5.6%. In the background, gas markets stayed volatile and bullish: Asian prices reached $29.30/MMBtu, and European prices hit their highest since December 2022 on Hormuz tanker attacks and strong cross-basin competition, with Morgan Stanley lifting its winter TTF forecast to €90/MWh. Spot tanker rates held at $20,500 (Atlantic) and eased to $27,000 (Pacific). UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, lost 6.97 points (3.0%) to close at 224.91 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 1.95%. The chart below illustrates the performance of both indices with weekly data. Week 42-2026: Chart of the UP World LNG Shipping Index with S&P 500 (Source: UP-Indices) Broader View Negative sentiment in equity markets affected the UPI, as shown by the UPI and S&P 500 charts. The median change in the UPI was -0.43 per cent, whilst the weighted index (wUPI) rose by 2.87 per cent. Taken together, these figures do not indicate particularly negative sentiment. The ratio of rising to falling index components was 10:11. Trading volume was above average, with above-average levels seen among both rising and falling stocks. The gas market remains volatile, fuelled by rising European purchases. The Reuters weekly summary, on which the rest of this section is based, states that Asian gas prices rose due to both repeated Iranian attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz and increasing European demand. The average Asian price reached $29.30/mmBtu. Despite an increase in transits via the Strait of Hormuz since September, as well as loadings at Qatar’s Ras Laffan facility, continued attacks on tankers and uncertainty over safe passage are keeping prices supported, he said. “With the disruption likely to persist into winter, competition for flexible LNG supply remains an important bullish factor,” said Arturo Regalado, senior LNG analyst at Kpler. Some tankers continue to leave the Gulf, but the situation remains volatile, said Alex Froley, senior LNG analyst at data intelligence firm ICIS. “The competition between Europe and Asia for flexible cargoes remains strong, as evidenced by increased mid-Atlantic course-change activity,” he added. The LNG tanker Shra’ouh, which was heading round Africa towards India, changed course back north, signalling a destination in the UK, but has recently turned south again, likely bound for Asia, Froley said. Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus, said Asian demand has been supported, with Chinese and South Korean buyers entering the market for spot cargoes, boosting competition between basins and driving European gas prices higher. In Europe, gas prices hovered around €88.57 per megawatt hour (MWh), or $29.20/mmBtu, on Friday afternoon, their highest intraday level since December 2022. “Even with recent warm weather and a recovery in Gulf LNG flows to 30 per cent of pre-conflict levels, our European region will still enter winter with storage at a record low of 74 per cent,” said Morgan Stanley analysts in a report. Morgan Stanley raised its winter TTF forecast to €90/MWh this week and said it could reach €135/MWh due to a combination of a prolonged outage in Qatar, colder weather or other LNG disruptions. S&P Global Energy assessed its daily Northwest Europe LNG price benchmark for cargoes delivered in November on an ex-ship basis at $27.825/mmBtu on Thursday, a $0.580/mmBtu discount to the front-month price at the Dutch TTF gas hub. Spot rates for LNG tankers remained at $20,500 per day for the Atlantic, whilst for the Pacific they fell to $27,000 per day, according to Spark Commodities. Constituents There were also two instances of double-digit growth, both in Asia. The larger of the two was recorded by Malaysia’s MISC (KLSE: 3816), which expanded its LNG fleet with a new tanker in October (under a contract with QatarEnergy) and has this year placed an order with Chinese shipyards for five new vessels under a 20-year contract with Petronas. Delivery is expected in 2030. According to TA, the strong 15.4 per cent rise in its share price took it out of a sideways range to its spring highs, closing just below its highest closing price without forming a wick at higher prices. Trading volume was slightly above average. The second company to post double-digit growth was South Korea’s Pan Ocean (KRX: 028670), which gained 11 per cent. During the week, however, its growth (in the short term) reached as high as 30 per cent. In any case, it has broken through all resistance levels, including key levels, and is continuing towards its pre-pandemic ranges. The next three major gains, of 8 per cent and 6 per cent, share a common thread, as they all relate to the oil and gas trio: BP (NYSE: BP; +8.6 per cent) easily broke through resistance (incidentally, the same level as in 2018), with the closing price and the high for the day being almost identical. Trading volume was slightly above average. Chevron (NYSE: CVX; +6.14 per cent) performed similarly, reaching new all-time highs. Shell (NYSE: SHEL) broke through resistance as early as the beginning of September and has now recorded a clear gain of 6.5 per cent. In its case, too, these are all-time highs. ALNG (OSE: ALNG) gained 1.5 per cent but continues to trade sideways. Given the company’s transformation from a pure transport operator (two TFDE LNG tankers on the spot market) to a gas trader with transport capacity, we expect a change in trend only once this transformation is complete. Exmar (EBR: EXM; +2.2 per cent) is undergoing a similarly subtle transformation, expanding its operations across the entire value chain from upstream to downstream. The share price is trading sideways. Other movements were less than 0.8 per cent. Korea Line Corporation (KRX: 005880) made an unsuccessful attempt to break out of its sideways range. Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (TSE: 9104) fared slightly better; while its attempt to break above the key resistance level was also unsuccessful, it closed above the range’s closing-price resistance level. “K” Line (TSE: 9107), on the other hand, closed within the range. All three Japanese companies – we’ll come back to NYK Line later – are trading within a sideways range at the highest price levels. This brings us to the falling companies. COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation (SS: 600026) suffered the heaviest losses, falling by almost 15 per cent. The chart remains unclear for now. The current uptrend was halted – and perhaps ended – after reaching spring levels. In any case, the price is now below spring levels. It was also the only double-digit decline. Flex LNG (NYSE: FLNG) and Dynagas LNG Partners (NYSE: DLNG) fell by 8 per cent. FLNG closed below the support level of its sideways range for the first time this year, suggesting a breakout. It reached the upper boundary of the previous sideways range’s high prices, but is also near the magnetic support level of the higher range. Given its high cash reserves, dividend payments are not at risk in the foreseeable future, so there is currently no reason for a sustained decline – apart from the general fall in share prices. DLNG fell to its lowest price level since 2024; trading volume was above average for both stocks. Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG; -5.6 per cent) also fell below its support level. This time, on higher volume, it also breached the magnetic support level. Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE) and New Fortress Energy (NASDAQ: NFE) both fell by four per cent. EE bounced off its support level after the decline, then rose slightly. The current trend is therefore sideways. NFE also showed a corrective decline, yet it has reached new lows. Nakilat (QSE: QGTS) closed near the previous week’s close, supported by a higher open. The company, affected by geopolitical tensions, thus lost only 1.8 per cent. This brings us to NYK Line (TSE: 9101), which fell 1.3% while trading in the upper range of its sideways channel on below-average volume. Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC) fell 1%, trading near the support level of its two-year sideways range. ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADX: ADNOCLS) remains at its major resistance level, down 0.9% after the rise the week before last. Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN) also fell 0.4 per cent after failing to break above resistance at its all-time high. It therefore remains within a short-term sideways range. The failed breakout appears linked more to the stock market decline than to a waning appetite for the company, given the above-average daily volume during the upward breakout. However, the following days saw the aforementioned return to the range. Crystal Ball Qatar remains sidelined among the conflict’s losers — but the key constraint is export, not production. The damage to Ras Laffan removed around 17% of capacity (two of 14 trains), which QatarEnergy expects to take three to five years to repair. The remaining ~80% of capacity is intact and could, in principle, return to market — but the Strait of Hormuz is Qatar’s sole export route, and executives (including Shell’s) caution that even a reopening would not restore pre-war flows overnight, as high war-risk insurance continues to deter tanker returns to the Gulf. For now, this keeps a large share of Qatari volume bottled up, and US LNG exporters emerge as the clear winners. European importers were shielded from spot price increases largely because of long-term US contracts; however, these are not enough to replenish winter inventories, and European companies must return to the market despite Qatar’s continuing export restrictions. We expect most of the rising US gas production to flow toward Europe. New global LNG producers should also benefit, as energy source diversification becomes more important than ever — provided importing economies remain healthy enough to absorb higher energy costs. The outlook remains volatile, but positive in the long term. The gradual phasing out of steam vessels and the addition of new liquefaction capacity will continue to drive the sector forward. articles.body: Platts increases standard ship size range for Asia-Pacific LNG cargo assessments in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, has increased the standard vessel size range reflected in its daily Asia-Pacific LNG cargo price assessments, effective Oct. 16. articles.title: The Grande Island: What you delete is only half the story
articles.summary: The recent decision in Olam International Ltd v Pacific Basin Supramax Ltd (The Grande Island) [2026] EWHC 2136 (Comm) concerned a familiar feature of charter partynegotiations where standard wording had been incorporated but parts of it deliberately deleted. The question was what those deletions meant for the...
articles.body: The Grande Island: What you delete is only half the story in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 The recent decision in Olam International Ltd v Pacific Basin Supramax Ltd (The Grande Island) [2026] EWHC 2136 (Comm) concerned a familiar feature of charter partynegotiations where standard wording had been incorporated but parts of it deliberately deleted. The question was what those deletions meant for the provisions left behind. Background The Grande Island was chartered under an amended NYPE form for a trip from Ghent to Nigeria. The charter party incorporated the BIMCO Piracy Clause for Time Charter Parties 2013, but sub-clauses 81(a) and (b) were expressly deleted. Had it remained, Clause 81(a) would have given Owners a broad right, based on the reasonable judgement of Owners or the Master, to refuse to proceed to or through an area considered dangerous because of piracy, or to leave such an area. Clause 81 (b) dealt with the alternative orders to be given by Charterers following the exercise of that right. Furthermore, Clause 81(c) was retained, and it allowed Owners, where the vessel proceeded to or through an area exposed to piracy risk, to take reasonable preventative measures to protect the vessel, crew and cargo. The clause gave examples of such measures, including re-routing, proceeding in convoy and adjusting speed or course, but this list was not exhaustive. After arriving off Warri, the vessel was unable to berth. Considering the background of piracy risk in the area, she left Warri and returned towards Lagos, before returning to Warri around three days later. The dispute was whether that temporary departure was permitted under Clause 81(c) and therefore whether the vessel remained on hire. Charterers’ case Charterers’ position centred on the parties’ decision to delete Clause 81(a) and (b). In their view, this was important because Clause 81(a) contained their express right for Owners to leave an area on account of piracy risk. Having specifically removed that right, Charterers argued that the more general wording of Clause 81(c) should not be interpreted as giving it back. They also relied on the types of preventative measures identified in Clause 81(c). Charterers argued that those examples were consistent with measures taken while navigating through or operating in the relevant area rather than leaving it altogether. On that construction, the vessel’s return towards Lagos was outside the protection of Clause 81(c) with Charterers maintaining that hire should not be payable for the concerned period. Owners’ case Owners’ case was that the deleted and retained provisions served different purposes. Clauses 81(a) and (b) provided broader rights, including a right triggered by the reasonable judgement of Owners or the Master. Clause 81(c) was narrower, requiring actual exposure to piracy risk, with any preventative measure taken also having to satisfy an objective standard of reasonableness. As such, the deletion of the broader rights did not mean that the parties had also removed the separate protection available under Clause 81(c). Furthermore, Owners relied on the breadth of the wording used in that provision and the fact that the listed preventative measures were examples rather than an exhaustive list. What did the Court decide? The arbitral tribunal found in Owners’ favour. It was satisfied that there was a piracy risk at Warri and that temporarily leaving the area was a reasonable preventative measure. Therefore, the vessel remained on hire. Charterers appealed under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1966, but the Commercial Court upheld the award. The Court considered the retained wording of Clause 81(c) sufficiently clear and broad to encompass leaving the area where doing so amounted to a reasonable preventative measure. The examples appearing in the clause did not confine the wider wording, particularly as the clause made clear that the measures identified were not exhaustive. Importantly, the Court did not treat the deletion of Clause 81(a) and Clause 81(b) as meaningless. Those provisions would have given Owners additional and more extensive rights. As a result, removing them changed the parties’ bargain but it did not narrow the separate right they had chosen to retain under Clause 81(c). Practical considerations for Charterers From a Charterers’ perspective, the case illustrates why amendments should be tested against the charter party as a whole. Removing one contractual right may not achieve the intended result if another provision can authorise similar conduct under a different test. This is particularly relevant where standard wording sits alongside bespoke rider clauses, as similar or overlapping rights may operate independently of each other. The treatment of the examples in Clause 81(c) is also worth noting. Where a contractual provision contains a broad right followed by a non-exhaustive list of examples, Charterers should be cautious about assuming that the right is confined to the situations expressly listed. If the parties intend the permitted measures to be limited to particular actions, clear wording may be required. At the fixture stage, the question should therefore not stop at what is being deleted. Charterers should also consider what rights remain and how they interact. If the commercial intention is that Owners should not be permitted to take a particular step, or that hire should cease if they do, it may be preferrable to address that consequence expressly. The decision is equally useful when a claim arises. If Owners rely on a safety or security clause to justify a diversion or other action, Charterers should focus on the particular requirements of that specific clause and the evidence supporting them. Here, the retained right depended on actual exposure to piracy risk and on the measure taken being reasonable. Those are matters capable of factual scrutiny, including what the risk was at the relevant time, what information was available to Owners and the Master, what alternatives were reasonably available and why the particular course was selected. Before making an off-hire deduction, Charterers should consider the charter party as a whole. Where another provision permits Owners to take the relevant action and expressly addresses the resulting allocation of time or hire, that provision may determine the position irrespective of the general off hire regime. Concluding, the drafting lesson from the Grande Island is a simple one. When negotiating what comes out of a charter party, equal attention should be paid to what stays in. Source: West of England 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Korea seeks dedicated US visa quota for shipbuilding workers in Shipbuilding News 20/10/2026 Korea is seeking a dedicated U.S. visa quota for shipbuilding workers as a condition for carrying out its $150 billion investment commitment under the Make American Shipbuilding Great Again (MASGA) initiative, according to the information submitted to Rep. Huh Sung-moo of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy. On Monday, Huh said that information he had received from the ministry indicated that it has been “explaining” to its U.S. counterparts the conditions “Washington needs to meet for Korea to fulfill its investment commitment.” “In particular, we have requested that the U.S. provide sufficient shipbuilding orders, allow joint shipbuilding through exemptions from restrictions on overseas construction, offer financial incentives and establish a dedicated visa quota for shipbuilding workers as prerequisites for implementing the investment commitment,” the ministry said in its response. The Korean government and business associations have been pushing for the introduction of a new E-4 visa category for Korean professionals in specialty occupations, but the proposal has yet to be enacted into law. In a separate response to Huh’s inquiry about whether the proposed shipbuilding visa quota would be separated from the E-4 visa, the ministry said it has “not made a specific request, but we believe that professional workers covered by the existing visa proposal and skilled technical workers needed at shipyards are different categories of workers.” “The number of workers needed will vary depending on the timing and progress of each investment project,” the ministry said. “At this stage, we believe establishing a visa route for workers to enter the U.S. is more important than specifying a number.” In a separate statement, the industry ministry said: “Led by the foreign ministry, Korea is discussing ways to improve the visa system to facilitate the entry and stay of Korean corporate personnel, including those in the shipbuilding sector.” The push for a dedicated visa quota for shipbuilding workers is key, as the sector accounts for $150 billion of Korea’s $350 billion investment commitment to the U.S., making it the largest single segment in the package. Compared with other areas of investment, shipbuilding offers more clearly defined areas of cooperation under a structure where Korean shipbuilders can directly benefit. To help revitalize the U.S. shipbuilding industry, skilled Korean workers will need to be deployed to American shipyards in the early stages to transfer their expertise and know-how. Personnel exchanges are also essential because the cooperation covers not only shipbuilding operations but also joint research and development projects. Currently, the Partner with Korea Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Young Kim, is pending in Congress. The bill seeks to establish a new visa category for Korean nationals working in specialty occupations, with an annual quota of up to 15,000 visas. Although versions of the bill have been introduced in successive sessions of Congress for more than a decade, it has yet to make significant progress. Even if the legislation advances, the quota would have to be shared across professions, potentially leaving insufficient slots for workers in shipbuilding. This appears to be one reason Korea is pushing for a separate, dedicated visa quota for the sector. “To maximize the benefits of the MASGA project, additional institutional measures are required,” Huh said. “Effective support measures, including visa negotiations, should be pursued to ensure that Korean workers can be employed at U.S. shipyards without difficulty.” Source: The Korea Times 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Panama bunker sales fall in September in Port News 20/10/2026 Changes in Panama bunker fuel sales from August to September: Total sales down 27,000 mt to 385,000 mt VLSFO sales up 19,000 mt to 266,000 mt LSMGO sales up 2,600 mt to 38,000 mt HSFO sales down 46,000 mt to 75,000 mt 0.5% MGO sales down 2,000 mt to 6,000 mt Panama’s bunker sales fell by around 7% in September from August, according to preliminary data from the Panama Maritime Authority. HSFO sales declined heavily in the month. The grade, which can only be burned by ships fitted with scrubbers to clean their exhaust, fell by around 38% to about 75,000 mt. This marks the grade’s lowest monthly volume since July 2023. The authority recorded no HSFO sales at all on the Atlantic side in September, against about 3,500 mt in August. Conversely, VLSFO sales moved the other way, rising by about 8%, to around 266,000 mt. LSMGO volumes also gained roughly 7%, while 0.5% MGO sales fell by about 28%. Total bunker sales averaged about 12,850 mt/day in September, compared to around 13,290 mt/day in August. Panama’s ports saw 543 ships call for bunkers in September, down from 569 in August and the fewest in any month since June 2024. The number of barges operating rose to 33 from 29. The average stem size, the volume lifted per ship, fell to around 710 mt in September, from 724 mt the previous month. VLSFO’s share of the market widened sharply, accounting for approximately 69% of total bunker sales. HSFO’s share narrowed to about 20% from around 29% in the previous month. Total MGO volumes made up roughly 11%. The bunker market in Panama is strong, and no weather disruptions are expected at Balboa and Cristobal. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal at both the ports, with recommended lead times of 3-6 days. HSFO needs slightly longer, with typical lead times of 4-7 days, a source said.
