articles.body: China unexpectedly increases its purchases of Brazilian oil in Freight News 20/10/2026 According to the South China Morning Post , amidst the turmoil in the global energy supply chain due to the conflict in the Gulf region, the Brazilian economy has seized a golden opportunity. According to a report by the Brazil-China Trade Council, bilateral trade reached a record high of $143 billion in the first nine months of the year. Brazilian crude oil exports to China hit a record high. A quarterly analysis based on official government data shows that the financial situation of this South American economy is very positive. Specifically, in the first nine months of the year, Brazil’s exports to China increased by 12%, reaching $84.7 billion . Conversely, imports of goods from China to Brazil also recorded an increase of nearly 10%, reaching $58.6 billion . The two-way trade deficit generated a trade surplus of $26.1 billion in just nine months, accounting for 42% of Brazil’s total trade surplus with the rest of the world . Crude oil contributed to these record-breaking figures, with exports to China surging 49% to a record $21.8 billion . This boom was driven by two main factors: increased shipping volumes and rising prices, both 27% and 17% respectively. China now holds half of Brazil’s total crude oil exports, nearly seven times the market share of India , the second-largest buyer. Despite international market fluctuations, Chinese customs data cited by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that China aggressively purchased oil from Brazil, even as its total crude oil imports fell by 32% in the second quarter. This strategic shift boosted Brazil’s total global crude oil exports by nearly 29%, reaching $43 billion . Not only China, but Brazil’s oil sales to India also saw a phenomenal 165% increase. The boom in the energy market has created a major shift in Brazil’s total export value. Reports show that oil now accounts for nearly 26% of the country’s total exports to China, up 6.3 percentage points from the previous year, and second only to its main export item, soybeans (which account for over 35%). Growth is slowing down. Besides the aforementioned export records, the figures for the first nine months of the year also show that Brazil’s export growth to China is slowing down. Specifically, this growth has slowed since the Council reported in July, when exports to China recorded a 22% increase. In contrast to the booming energy market, the beef market recorded a decline, negatively impacting Brazil’s revenue. Specifically, the country’s beef exports fell by 8.5%, to $5.5 billion , accompanied by a 22% decrease in volume. This was due to Brazil reaching its annual quota of 1.1 million tons under protectionist regulations from the Chinese market. According to the report, China dropped to fifth place among countries buying Brazilian beef in September, accounting for only 5.6% of total consumption, behind the US with a market share of 21.5%. Conversely, electric vehicles were the biggest driver of Brazil’s import growth from China. The country’s purchases of plug-in hybrid vehicles increased by 89%, reaching $2.87 billion , while battery-powered electric vehicles saw a 341% increase, reaching approximately $2.4 billion . Conventional hybrid vehicles currently account for about one-tenth of Brazil’s total vehicle imports from China. Brazilian brands hold 86% of the electric vehicle market share that Brazil imports from overseas. In response to significant market fluctuations, BYD – China’s largest automaker in Brazil – proactively shipped large consignments ahead of the surge in demand and began assembling electric vehicles directly at its factory in Camaçari, Bahia state. Besides the aforementioned key products, the report also noted the initial positive results of the Chinese market’s opening to Brazilian agricultural products. Specifically, revenue from sorghum reached $170 million , with the Chinese market currently consuming 95% of Brazil’s total sorghum exports. Simultaneously, exports of spodumene, a lithium-containing mineral, from the South American nation also increased by 339%, reaching $172.3 million , with 97% of production destined for China. articles.body: Asia Environment Finance and Insurance Tankers Tech Eastern Pacific links wind propulsion repayments to fuel savings Bojan Lepic October 20, 2026 0 205 1 minute read EPS EPS Singapore-based Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has secured financing for wind-assisted propulsion systems on two vessels through a fund linking repayments to independently verified fuel savings. The Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET), managed by AIM Horizon Investments with the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) as decarbonisation adviser, is making its first deployment with the EPS projects. The vessels, Pacific Sentinel and Pacific Sunstone , have each been fitted with three 22-metre suction sails, making them the first ships in the EPS fleet to adopt wind-assisted propulsion. FEET offers up to 100% upfront financing for energy efficiency technologies, with shipowners making payments based on verified fuel and regulatory savings. The financing model builds on earlier trials involving GCMD and EPS aboard Pacific Sentinel , during which researchers collected 276m data points over four months of trading in the Americas between May and September 2025. The analysis examined 203 valid sail on-off transitions to isolate the technology’s impact on fuel consumption from changing operating conditions. The methodology has undergone independent review, with future project savings subject to verification before payments are calculated. “Decarbonisation moves faster when the technology, the data, and the financing come together,” said EPS chief executive Cyril Ducau. The fund is backed by the Development Bank of Japan, DBS Bank and ING, with the partners aiming to expand the financing model to other energy efficiency technologies across shipping fleets. articles.body: CMA CGM has announced Port Congestion Surcharges (PCS) for shipments to three West African ports: Tema in Ghana, Freetown in Sierra Leone and Monrovia in Liberia. The charges will take effect on November 1, 2026, based on the loading date. For shipments from the United States and Brazil, they will apply from November 15. The carrier said the surcharges reflect current operating conditions at the three ports. New congestion charges for Tema For dry containers shipped to Tema, CMA CGM will apply a surcharge of €200 or US$200 per container, depending on the origin. Shipments from the Far East will face a charge of US$200 per TEU. Refrigerated containers will face higher charges of €850 or US$1,000 per TEU. The surcharge covers shipments from several regions, including the Far East, Europe, the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Americas. Freetown and Monrovia surcharges For shipments to Freetown, the surcharge will depend on the region of origin. Cargo from Northern Europe, the Western Mediterranean, the Adriatic and North Africa will face a charge of €350 per TEU. Shipments from North America, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Black Sea will be subject to US$400 per TEU. A higher surcharge of US$700 per TEU will apply to shipments from the Far East, Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and specified regions of the Americas. All three rates cover dry, refrigerated and special equipment. For Monrovia, dry containers from Northern Europe, the Western Mediterranean, the Adriatic and North Africa will face a charge of €250 per container. The surcharge for refrigerated cargo from these regions will be €600 per TEU. Shipments from the Far East, Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf, North America, South America, Eastern Mediterranean and Black Sea, along with specified Central American and Caribbean origins, will face charges of US$300 per dry container or US$700 per reefer TEU. CMA CGM confirmed that the congestion charges will be collected together with the freight payment.
takeaways: CMA CGM has announced Port Congestion Surcharges (PCS) for shipments to three West African ports: Tema in Ghana, Freetown in Sierra Leone and Monrovia in Liberia.
The charges will take effect on November 1, 2026, based on the loading date.
For shipments from the United States and Brazil, they will apply from November 15.

articles.title: US moves to legitimise shadow tanker fleet
articles.summary: The Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers to approved investors who would refurbish the vessels and return them to legitimate crude trades, US energy secretary Chris Wright revealed yesterday, as Washington scrambles to contain soaring freight costs amid the Hormuz crisis. Speaking at...
articles.body: Americas Europe Regulatory Tankers US moves to legitimise shadow tanker fleet Sam Chambers October 20, 2026 0 1,672 2 minutes read Greenpeace Greenpeace The Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers to approved investors who would refurbish the vessels and return them to legitimate crude trades, US energy secretary Chris Wright revealed yesterday, as Washington scrambles to contain soaring freight costs amid the Hormuz crisis. Speaking at a Citadel Securities event in New York, Wright said the government was developing an approval process for formerly blacklisted vessels to trade under recognised owners, carrying only non-sanctioned oil. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’” he said. Wright insisted the move was not a blanket lifting of sanctions on Iranian or Russian oil, describing it instead as the conversion of ships into legitimate assets. He put the global dark fleet at around 1,600 tankers and suggested “dozens” or possibly “hundreds” might eventually re-enter compliant trading. Tanker owners’ association INTERTANKO has pushed back hard, warning that legalising a vessel does not automatically address its condition, ownership or insurance. “If additional tanker capacity is required, policy should encourage cargoes towards the quality, compliant fleet,” the association said. INTERTANKO warned that opaque insurance arrangements, weak oversight and missing inspection histories pose risks to crews, the environment and coastal states, while sending the wrong signal to owners that have invested heavily in safety and compliance. Market analysts are equally sceptical about whether the initiative can meaningfully depress extraordinary freight rates. Kpler estimates only 24 of roughly 160 OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs could realistically return to mainstream trading after ownership and age restrictions are considered. It argued yesterday that war risk around the Middle East Gulf, rather than vessel numbers alone, is driving freight costs, and that loosening sanctions could weaken geopolitical leverage without delivering meaningful relief.\ Braemar put the potential increase even lower at just 19 VLCCs once vessels tied to Iran and European sanctions are excluded. Braemar stressed that any lasting impact depends on Hormuz flows and how long Washington’s approval arrangements remain in place. Arrow Research’s filtering has produced a maximum of 22 eligible tankers across all sizes, including 14 VLCCs, and none in the suezmax or aframax segments. Arrow sees continued upside risk for freight, with the strong market potentially extending through the first quarter of 2027 as shuttle operations, ship-to-ship transfers and security risks keep tonnage tied up. BRS, meanwhile, has identified 148 deepsea tankers sanctioned by the US alone, representing just 2.5% of the global deepsea fleet. Only 14 appear to have been idle for more than three months. Most of the remainder are already working in grey trades, while UK and EU restrictions could prevent them obtaining essential insurance and other maritime services. BRS maintained that Washington’s initiative is unlikely to have a significant immediate impact on freight rates, with the majority of potentially eligible tonnage already employed and the fundamental constraints on tanker movements through Hormuz remaining unresolved. The shadow fleet move follows Washington’s decision earlier this month to temporarily authorise Russian diesel trade until April 7, 2027, drawing criticism from Kyiv and US lawmakers. articles.title: Folegandros island joins Greece’s mainland power grid via 60-kilometer subsea cable
articles.summary: The new 60-kilometer subsea high-voltage cable that connects the Greek island of Folegandros with Santorini and Naxos has been energized and is...
articles.body: Interconnectors October 20, 2026 · 7 hours ago Folegandros island joins Greece’s mainland power grid via 60-kilometer subsea cable NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email IPTO The new 60-kilometer subsea high-voltage cable that connects the Greek island of Folegandros with Santorini and Naxos has been energized and is now part of the mainland power grid, the Greek electricity grid operator Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO) reported. The link is part of the Southern Cyclades electrical interconnection project, whose construction was completed early this summer, connecting Santorini, Folegandros, Milos and Serifos to the mainland power system via Attica. The Southern Cyclades project marks the fourth and final phase of the program that aims to reshape the energy infrastructure of the Cyclades. With a total budget of €385.7 million, the project includes 294 kilometers of high-voltage submarine and underground cables and four fully digital gas-insulated substations (GIS). The substation constructed to supply Folegandros with electricity is one of the four that incorporate the GIS technology. "The interconnection of the Southern Cyclades, which completes the integration of the island group into the high-voltage grid, was a technically complex project that enhanced IPTO's expertise. With the energization of the interconnections for Santorini, Milos, and Serifos in the coming period, we are closing another major chapter of energy projects in the Aegean," said IPTO's Chairman and CEO Manos Manousakis on October 19. The project is co-funded by the EU through the Greece 2.0 Recovery and Resilience Facility and is also financed through loans from the European Investment Bank (EIB) and additional resources from the RRF. articles.body: Containers Europe Greater China Shipyards MSC tipped for another 20 megamaxes in China Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 1,236 1 minute read Yangzijiang Shipbuilding Yangzijiang Shipbuilding Mediterranean Shipping Co (MSC) has reportedly added another 20 megamax containerships at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries, further expanding its already massive orderbook as global newbuilding commitments climb to their highest level in more than a decade. According to liner consultancy Linerlytica, Gianluigi Aponte’s carrier has booked 20 additional 24,000 teu vessels at the Dalian-based shipbuilder, representing another 480,000 teu of future capacity. The latest deal takes MSC’s programme of vessels exceeding 20,000 teu at Hengli to 62 ships, Linerlytica said in its latest weekly market report. No contract value, delivery dates or propulsion specifications have been disclosed for the new batch. MSC has built up a substantial pipeline at Hengli since the two companies signed a strategic cooperation agreement in 2024. The liner giant initially contracted ten 21,000 teu and ten 24,000 teu LNG dual-fuel newbuildings, before returning for six 22,000 teu ships last year. The latest reported order adds another sizeable block of capacity to an expansion programme that already dwarfs those of rival carriers. At the end of September, Alphaliner data cited by Splash put MSC’s operated fleet at around 7.4m teu, representing 21.5% of global liner capacity, with another 2.94m teu on order. Its combined fleet and orderbook had already passed the 10m teu mark. MSC’s latest move comes amid a renewed surge in container newbuilding activity. Linerlytica estimates the global containership orderbook has reached 16.2m teu, equivalent to 46.5% of the existing fleet, the highest ratio since 2009. South Korea’s HMM is also pressing ahead with its fleet expansion, confirming contracts worth about KRW1.92trn ($1.44bn) for eight 13,000 teu LNG dual-fuel containerships at HD Hyundai. Six vessels will be built at HD Hyundai Samho and two at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, with deliveries starting in 2029. HMM plans to deploy the ships on its Far East–India–Mediterranean service. The Korean carrier has also acquired four feeder vessels through resale agreements, comprising three 2,800 teu ships and one of 1,700 teu. articles.summary: Japan-headquartered Sumitomo Electric Industries has held the opening ceremony for what is said to be the UK's first HVDC subsea cable factory,...
articles.body: Cabling October 20, 2026 · 8 hours ago UK’s first HVDC subsea cable factory opens in Scotland NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Sumitomo Electric Japan-headquartered Sumitomo Electric Industries has held the opening ceremony for what is said to be the UK's first HVDC subsea cable factory, located at the Port of Nigg in Scotland. The factory, located within the Inverness and Cromarty Firth Green Freeport boundary, represents an investment of £350 million (over €416 million) in the local Highlands economy. The opening ceremony that took place on October 19 included Japanese cultural heritage with local Scottish traditions, featuring the ceremonial Kagami Biraki - the breaking open of sake casks with wooden mallets for good fortune - alongside bagpipe performances. “I am delighted to celebrate the official opening of our new subsea cable factory in Scotland, following the announcement of its establishment in April 2023 and the groundbreaking ceremony held in May 2024. This factory will serve as a vital production base supporting the strengthening of the UK’s transmission infrastructure, the expansion of renewable energy deployment, and the delivery of a stable and reliable energy supply for generations to come," said Osamu Inoue, President of Sumitomo Electric Industries. “Building on more than a century of experience and technological expertise in subsea cable systems, we remain committed to supporting interconnector and offshore wind projects across Europe. By helping connect the energy networks of the future, we will continue contributing to the development of a more sustainable society.” The new plant covers 58,000 square meters of floor space on a 15-hectare site. It will manufacture 525 kV XLPE HVDC subsea transmission cables and subsea inter-array cables. According to Sumitomo, the facility will directly create over 200 skilled local jobs, with a total projected impact of over 400 jobs across the broader UK supply chain. This will be supported by a “Train the Trainer” model and operator training programs conducted in Japan. “This facility puts Scotland right at the heart of the energy transition and is a strong vote of confidence in our people, skills and engineering excellence. We invested £24.5 million in its construction to support hundreds of well-paid jobs in the Highlands and create lasting opportunities for future generations," said First Minister of Scotland John Swinney . “As the first factory of its kind in the UK, it will help unlock our enormous offshore wind potential while bolstering energy security. We will continue to do all we can to create jobs, drive growth and build on Scotland’s position as the UK's leading destination for inward investment outside London.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! REUTERS/Khalil Ashawi By Ari Natter and Annmarie Hordern (Bloomberg) — The Trump administration is authorizing the sale of sanctioned oil tankers in an effort to allow the vessels to start legitimately shipping crude, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. The US government is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use the ships to transport non-sanctioned oil, Wright said Monday at a Citadel Securities event in New York. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’ ” Wright said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore.” Wright’s comments represent the first detailed public explanation from the Trump administration about turning to sanctioned tankers as it seeks to expand the number of ships available to transport crude and boost supply disrupted by the war in Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump administration is undertaking an approval process to grant ships legitimate status, Wright said. He rejected the idea that the US was simply removing sanctions from tankers that carried crude from nations such as Russia or Iran. “We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers,” Wright said. “There is no removing of sanctions.” The move comes as Republicans in the US confront voters who are concerned about higher fuel costs weeks before midterm elections. Gasoline and diesel prices surged following the Mideast conflict adding a pain point for voters already worried about affordability. Wright estimated that there are about 1,600 vessels in the global “dark fleet” of sanctioned tankers. The Trump administration’s effort to convert those into lawful ships could ultimately add “dozens” or even “hundreds” of tankers to the legitimate fleet, he said. The perils of transporting oil through the strait have sent shipping fees skyrocketing. Moving oil from the Persian Gulf to East Asia costs more than six times as much as it did prior to the conflict. More than 40% of the world’s fleet of about 850 very large crude carriers are now either in the Persian Gulf or within a couple of days sailing time from it, according to Signal Ocean, a shipping data provider. In addition, Wright said during the wide-ranging interview that part of the reason the Trump administration agreed to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release the country’s diesel supplies into global markets in a widely criticized move was to provide an incentive for the Kremlin to end the war with Ukraine. “If you can produce more diesel than you consume, you can export it to the world. Well, what’s their route to do that? They can they can end the conflict in Ukraine,” Wright said. “That would be a real plus. They could get an energy ceasefire with the Ukrainians and fix their refineries, or they can reduce their consumption of diesel for war fighting activities. So if they change their behavior, and all of these are steps towards peace in the conflict, and you have surplus diesel, where you can export it to the world.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: Congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration’s Jones Act waiver is growing, with Rep. Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) demanding answers about whether foreign vessels operating in domestic U.S. trades are complying with...

Join the leading maritime news network The Soho Square, a crude oil tanker sailing under the flag of Liberia, is at anchor in the Galveston Bay as it makes it’s way to the Port of Houston shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a 60-day waiver of the Jones Act shipping law, in Texas City, Texas, U.S. March 18, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian Congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration’s Jones Act waiver is growing, with Rep. Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) demanding answers about whether foreign vessels operating in domestic U.S. trades are complying with immigration, tax and maritime laws. In an October 16 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, first reported Monday by Bloomberg Government , Carbajal raised concerns about the administration’s oversight of the waiver, particularly following reports that foreign-flagged tankers had transported millions of dollars worth of petroleum products between U.S. ports without making required disclosures. The letter follows reporting by gCaptain in September that identified evidence of 14 previously unreported domestic tanker voyages, plus a possible 15th, expanding on an earlier Bloomberg Government investigation that found at least a dozen foreign vessels had moved more than $40 million in petroleum products without appearing in the Maritime Administration’s (MARAD) public waiver records. The missing voyages raised questions about how much foreign-vessel activity was actually taking place under the emergency waiver. A gCaptain review of MARAD’s September 16 data counted 255 reported movements under the original March 17 waiver and its May extension, but the additional voyages suggested that figure was incomplete. MARAD previously told Bloomberg Government that it lacks the legal authority to compel vessel operators to submit the required reports. Enforcement of the Jones Act falls to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which operates under DHS. Carbajal, the ranking Democrat on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee’s Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, is now seeking answers about whether other federal requirements are being enforced. “These reports raise significant questions about whether DHS and its component agencies are adequately enforcing federal law with respect to foreign vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce,” Carbajal wrote. One concern involves the immigration status of foreign seafarers working aboard vessels making domestic voyages. Federal immigration regulations generally prohibit foreign crewmembers admitted under D nonimmigrant status from working in connection with domestic vessel movements. Carbajal asked DHS and CBP to explain how they are applying that restriction to foreign officers and crewmembers aboard ships operating under the waiver, and what legal authority permits them to work on those voyages. He also requested information about any cases in which crewmembers were found to have immigration status inconsistent with domestic service, or had absconded from their vessels, along with any resulting enforcement actions. The letter also raises tax questions following recent Internal Revenue Service guidance clarifying that income earned by foreign corporations transporting cargo between U.S. ports under the waiver is considered domestic-source income and does not qualify for the international shipping income exclusion under Section 883 of the Internal Revenue Code or related treaty benefits. Carbajal wants to know whether DHS has coordinated with the Treasury Department and IRS to identify foreign vessel owners, operators and charterers using the waiver, including whether agencies have shared voyage dates, cargo movements and other information needed to determine potential tax obligations. He also requested details on DHS enforcement of other requirements covering maritime security, environmental protection, vessel safety and inspection, wages, labor and employment, customs and harbor maintenance. The latest questions come as the administration has tightened the waiver process. A second 90-day extension, which took effect August 17, requires operators to first submit a Vessel Availability Request so the government can determine whether a qualified U.S.-flagged vessel is available before authorizing foreign tonnage. Carbajal said publicly available information indicates that more than 25 domestic voyages have been completed under the current waiver, including multiple voyages by some vessels. The waiver was originally issued in March amid energy supply disruptions stemming from the war with Iran. The current extension runs through November 15. “The Administration has now authorized the waiver for an aggregate period of approximately 250 days, making oversight particularly important,” Carbajal wrote. “Congress has a responsibility to ensure that a national-defense waiver is not being treated as a broader exemption from federal law.” Carbajal requested a response by October 31, including details about coordination between DHS and the Departments of Defense, Transportation and Treasury, the IRS and Coast Guard. According to Bloomberg Government, DHS declined to comment and referred questions to the Department of Defense, which did not respond to a request for comment. Join the leading maritime news network A view shows the Russian ice-class Arctic LNG carrier Nikolay Yevgenov is mangaed by Teekay, flagged Bahamas, and is classified by Russian Maritime Register of Shipping REUTERS/Stephane Mahe Oct 19 (Reuters) – Russia’s oil exports through its Northern Sea Route (NSR) in 2026 have already exceeded last year’s by nearly 50%, with some 20 million barrels shipped to Asia from the start of navigation in July to mid-October, traders said and data showed. The NSR links Russia’s western ports with Asian markets through icy Arctic waters and is considered a more dangerous and expensive route. This year, however, it became more attractive as a result of disruptions to routes via the Suez Canal, the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea area, traders said. Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, driving them to ?seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. This made high tariffs for ships using the NSR, which requires assistance from an icebreaker, less costly compared with the usual route to Asia through the Red Sea, traders said. For Russia, which controls the NSR, it represents a secure alternative to European waters, where tankers with its oil have been regularly arrested this year. The volume of Russian oil exported through the Arctic route is expected to rise by another 5-10 million barrels by the end of the navigation period, traders’ preliminary estimates show. Russia shipped 13 million barrels during the last navigation season. Gazprom Neft, one of Russia’s oil majors, will increase its shipments via the NSR by some 35% this year compared with 2025, its CEO Alexander Dyukov told journalists on Friday in Moscow. Russia also supplies significant volumes of LNG to Asia via the NSR as well as other goods. LNG supply via the NSR is also expected to rise this year after the launch of Arctic LNG shipments. President Vladimir Putin told an economic forum in Vladivostok in September that Russia expects cargo turnover via the NSR to double to 70 million metric tons annually by the end of the decade. Rosneft’s giant new oil project in the north of Russia, Vostok Oil, which opened last month, is already contributing to the rising volumes using the NSR. articles.summary: Iran’s main oil-loading terminals have remained empty for weeks, adding to signs that a US naval blockade of the country is throttling Tehran’s exports.

U.S. Central Command Photo (Bloomberg) — Iran’s main oil-loading terminals have remained empty for weeks, adding to signs that a US naval blockade of the country is throttling Tehran’s exports. No tankers have docked at Kharg Island’s crude-export terminals since late August, an analysis of ship-tracking data and European Union satellite images shows. That’s the longest stretch of inactivity at the island since the start of the US-Iran war in February. The lack of tankers at Kharg, deep inside the Persian Gulf, points to the increasing pressure on Iran since the US renewed its military blockade of the country’s shipping three months ago. Crude exports have plunged from almost 1 million barrels a day in July to nothing since late August, according to vessel-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg and figures from Kpler and Vortexa. July’s loadings were concentrated in the first half of the month, after a ceasefire deal between Washington and Tehran temporarily lifted the US blockade. No tankers laden with Iranian crude have managed to leave the country or nearby waters since the middle of that month, when the shipping ban was reimposed, nonprofit group United Against Nuclear Iran said. Iran exported nearly 650 million barrels of crude in the year through April, with most ending up in China, tanker-tracking data show. Now, as Tehran’s oil disappears from global markets, Chinese refiners are turning to other sources of crude and competing with other buyers for barrels and ships. That’s pushed oil prices higher and fueled a historic rally in freight. As Iran has been thwarted in its attempts to export its production, Tehran has stepped up attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the open seas. In the first two weeks of October, 25 ships were targeted in and around the chokepoint, compared with 18 incidents reported for the whole of September and 15 in August, according to alerts sent out by UK Maritime Trade Operations, a unit of the country’s navy. Kharg Island handles almost all of Iran’s crude exports, with Jask — a port at the eastern end of Hormuz — accounting for just a small percentage of the trade. While Kharg has been idle, no tankers have been seen berthed at Jask either, the satellite images show. The images reviewed by Bloomberg News were taken from the EU’s Sentinel 1 and 2 orbiters. They pass separately over the island every few days, and the longest gap between any of their images was three days. It typically takes about 24 to 48 hours to fully load a very large crude carrier at Kharg Island. A small ship appeared berthed on Oct. 10, seemingly breaking the 40-day period of dormancy. But its automated position signals identified it as the chemicals/products tanker Clavel, which has been shuttling between Iranian ports. Separately, at least two tankers were seen docked at jetties off Kharg Island’s southeast tip between Sept. 12 and Sept. 15, but those are only used to handle shipments of liquefied petroleum gas and sulfur. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The Trump administration has scheduled the first offshore mineral lease sale in U.S. history, opening more than 31 million acres of seabed near American Samoa to companies seeking critical minerals...

The Trump administration has scheduled the first offshore mineral lease sale in U.S. history, opening more than 31 million acres of seabed near American Samoa to companies seeking critical minerals from the deep ocean. The Department of the Interior’s Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) on Monday issued its Final Leasing Notice for the November 19 auction, clearing the final major administrative step before companies can bid on rights to explore and potentially develop mineral deposits on the U.S. Outer Continental Shelf. The sale, designated PACM-1, includes two lease areas covering approximately 31.5 million acres. The larger area encompasses 16.3 million acres, while the second covers 15.2 million acres. Under the final lease terms, each area carries a minimum bid of $3 million and a primary lease term of 20 years. Production royalties would begin at 2% for the first five years of commercial mining, increasing to 5% thereafter. The areas contain potential deposits of polymetallic nodules and ferromanganese crusts, which can hold valuable minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. The Trump administration has made expanding domestic supplies of critical minerals a national security priority, particularly as it seeks to reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains. “Critical minerals are no longer just commodities; they are a vital strategic asset in global competition,” said acting MMA Director Mike Olsen. Olsen said the agency also recognizes the cultural, economic and environmental importance of the waters surrounding American Samoa and would balance mineral development with environmental safeguards and engagement with local communities. Importantly, winning a lease would not immediately authorize mining. According to MMA, leaseholders would initially be permitted to conduct preliminary activities such as mapping and environmental surveys. More extensive exploration, testing and commercial mineral extraction would require separate federal approvals and environmental reviews. The agency has completed an environmental assessment of the leasing proposal and issued a finding of no significant impact for the initial activities. The announcement nevertheless drew sharp criticism from environmental groups, which have opposed opening the deep ocean to commercial mining before its ecological impacts are fully understood. “These lease sales will open the floodgates to the exploitation of our deep seas,” said Oceana Defense Campaign Manager Julia Singer. Singer accused the administration of disregarding opposition from scientists, local leaders and communities concerned about the potential environmental consequences. Oceana said the proposed lease areas are near Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a protected marine area that provides habitat for sea turtles, humpback whales and other species. Deep-sea mining could involve remotely operated machines collecting mineral-rich nodules from the seabed or removing crusts from underwater rock formations. Environmental groups warn that these operations could destroy seafloor habitats and create sediment plumes that affect marine life beyond the immediate mining sites. The leasing proposal has also raised concerns in American Samoa, where fisheries are a major part of the local economy. In comments submitted during the leasing process, American Samoa Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula called for stronger environmental monitoring, protections for tuna fisheries and greater oversight of vessels using Pago Pago Harbor. The governor also urged federal officials to consider the cumulative effects of mining-related vessel traffic, including potential pressure on port infrastructure, waste management and water quality. His comments emphasized that any future commercial extraction must be considered separately from the lease sale and should not be treated as an inevitable outcome. MMA said it had incorporated the governor’s recommendations where permitted by law or would address them during subsequent regulatory reviews. The governor also requested a share of federal mineral leasing revenues for American Samoa. In its response, MMA acknowledged that existing law does not currently provide authority for such revenue sharing. The latest announcement follows a series of steps by the Trump administration to establish a domestic offshore minerals industry. The government is also advancing a separate mineral leasing proposal near the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, while NOAA has been processing applications for deep-sea mineral exploration in international waters under U.S. law. MMA was established in July through the reunification of the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, bringing offshore leasing and safety oversight back under a single agency. The American Samoa auction is scheduled for November 19, with the final notice set for publication in the Federal Register on October 20. Whether the sale ultimately leads to commercial mining remains uncertain, but it marks a significant step in Washington’s effort to develop a U.S. deep-sea minerals industry. Source: Minesto The European Commission has selected Swedish ocean energy developer Minesto for a €20.2 million Innovation Fund grant for the company's planned 10 MW tidal kite array in Ireland. Minesto now enters the Grant Agreement Preparation (GAP) phase for the grant that will cover 60% of the needed investment for the proposed Euro Dragon Farm. The grant agreement will be signed with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA), with the process expected to be finalized in the first quarter of 2027. “Being selected for this 20.2 M EUR grant contribution to our latest project development opportunity, the Euro Dragon Farm, is the most significant commercial milestone in Minesto’s history so far. Our dragon technology competitiveness, attractiveness of the Dragon Farm investment case and our assessed project execution capability have been highly rated, resulting in Minesto being selected to spearhead the commercial build-out of Europe's tidal energy sector," said Martin Edlund , CEO of Minesto. To be located in Irish coastal waters, Euro Dragon Farm is the EU's first Dragon Farm tidal energy project. The grant is part of a wider funding support program, under which the European Commission selected 77 European net-zero technology projects to receive funding support worth €3.4 billion under the call launched in December 2025. The Commission estimates that the projects have the potential to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions, avoiding the equivalent of around 290 million tons over their first decade of operations.
